claims.statement: Told his men the Liang troops were shop boys in fine armor, then advised Zhuangzong to pull back and wait.

Argued that cavalry wins on open ground and that the riverbank was the wrong place.
Turned away displeased and lay down in his tent; no general dared go in.
Told Zhang Chengye that holding back was not fear and that they should withdraw to Haoyi and tire the enemy.
Told Zhuangzong that Dewei was a veteran who knew war and should not be dismissed.
Sat up and said he was thinking the same thing; later laughed that it was just as Dewei said.

Sent three hundred riders to taunt the Liang camp and followed with three thousand men. Those are counts, not years.
Marched out in fury with his whole host and skirmished with Dewei to south of Haoyi.
Rejoiced at the open ground and told Dewei he would lead.
Urged waiting until the hungry Liang troops pulled back; the other commanders agreed. They are not named.
Charged with drums and cries, shouting that Wei and Hua were running, and Liang's lines broke.
Was routed from Gaoyi to Baixiang and escaped with a dozen riders.

claims.assessment: His loyalty in crying rebellion and cutting his hair deserves praise, but he fled instead of dying and his death was not the one he had sworn.
Fierce and resolute, he excelled at mounted archery and was famed for taking prisoners alive.

claims.statement: Struck undefended Taiyuan, and his army broke when Jinquan attacked at night.
Led office craftsmen onto the walls, then rejoiced and armed Jinquan.
Told Chengye that Taiyuan was Jin's foundation and that he could still break the enemy.
With more than a hundred sons, kin, and old officers went out the north gate and broke Wang Tan in the Sheep-Horse city. The kin are not named.
Never recorded Jinquan's merit.

label.en: military governor of the Zhenwu Army

claims.statement: recalled to the capital after two years in command and died of illness. Two years is a span.
Campaigned against Huang Chao to Huayin and took in the nine-year-old Jianfeng. Nine is an age.

label.en: chief adjutant of the Iron Forest

claims.statement: Fought Wang Xingyu and Li Kuangwei, broke the twin fortifications, and fought at Baixiang.

label.en: commander of the left wing horse army
deputy to the Inner Gate director of command

claims.statement: Struck Wang Qian, took more than a thousand heads and seventy officers. Those are counts.
Seized Xiang and rebelled; Jianfeng crushed him.
Recalled Jianfeng for old kindness, visited his home, and honored him.

label.en: titular military governor of the Zhennan Army

claims.statement: died drawing the salary granted him

unresolvedReferences.description: The Prince of Jin is not named. No personal name is supplied.
Fifty thousand is a count. Han here is the ethnic group, not a person.

冬 is kept unresolved. Five li is a distance.
Divine Might, Dragon Soar, and Bent Bow are army corps, not people.
Dewei calls the ruler the king, 王. That generic title is not given a surface. It refers in context to Zhuangzong, who had just withdrawn to his tent.
未申時 is a time of day, not a date.
The English writes Gaoyi here and Haoyi elsewhere for 鄗. Both are places. A dozen riders is a count.
Decades and dozens of battles are spans and counts, not years.
Thirty thousand is a count. Yan here is the state, not Liu Yan.
More than a year is a span, not a Western year.
十五年 is kept unresolved. The unit names no era, and none is supplied.
Two days is a span.
Dewei addresses the ruler as 王, English Majesty. That generic title is not given a surface; in context it is Zhuangzong.
The English Li Cun’an renders 李存審. s0095 says Cunshen was given the surname Li and named Cunshen, so 李存審 is linked to Fu Cunshen. Strongly inferred; the English spelling is kept as written.
